subsubtopic: INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING-REQUEST FOR DEBATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 26, I ask leave to propose a motion to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, Sir, the unprecedented increase in the cost of living.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING-REQUEST FOR DEBATE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham has filed with the Chair the notice required under Standing Order 26. He has also left with me additional written submissions in support of the motion, which material has been considered carefully. The hon. member proposes that the House set aside the government business intended for consideration later today, to provide an opportunity to debate the "unprecedented increase", to use his words, in the cost of living announced by Statistics Canada. Obviously, this is a matter of the first importance and concern to the House, and I should think that many members would hope that such a debate would take place soon.
The Standing Order imposes on the Chair the duty to consider as a primary factor whether there will be an opportunity for debate within a reasonable period of time. The information I have indicates that the special committee on the trends in food prices will be reporting to the House soon, probably within the next week. It is assumed that a motion to concur in the report will be placed on the order paper by the chairman, or perhaps by some other member of the committee, and debated. It seems to me that hon. members would prefer to debate this important and urgent issue in this way rather than under an adjournment motion.
My suggestion is, of course, predicated on the assumption that the committee will report very soon so that a motion to concur in that report can be debated. If such a report were not forthcoming, the circumstances would become materially altered and the advisability of a debate under the terms of Standing Order 26, as suggested by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, or by another procedure, could then be reviewed. For the moment, in view of the fact there is this probable opportunity for debate within a reasonable time, I would think the Chair should not allow the motion to be put, at least for today.

July 10, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
f English]

The House resumed, from Monday, July 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-208, to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject we are debating under this bill has been a parliamentary issue since the eighteenth century when the pattern of population changed in Great Britain. Industrial towns and cities were created which had few representatives in the British parliament; large rural areas with few people in them had many members in parliament. This issue which was debated in the British House almost two centuries ago resulted in reform which recognized the principle to which I was referring at the time of adjournment last night, namely, representation by population.
It was recognized in reforming the centuries-old composition of the British House that fundamentally a democratic legislature had to give priority to representation by population and that new representation opportunities had to be accorded the cities and the towns which the industrial revolution had created.
What happened in the eighteenth century in Great Britain has been reflected in the parliamentary history of our own country. The issue with which we are concerned in this debate is older than confederation. Indeed, the phrase "representation by population", or its abbreviation "rep by pop", goes back to the time of the United Province of Canada when the growth of the western part of the province exceeded that of the east. This brought about a desire for change in the composition of the Parliament of Canada which gave equal membership to both parts of the province. It was then recognized that some consideration had to be given to population changes and that increased representation had to be provided when there was a major increase in population.
This issue that was before the people of Canada before confederation was fundamental in drawing up the terms of union that were expressed in the British North America Act. We see in that act, which is to such a large degree the constitution of our country, the way in which the membership of the Parliament of Canada recognizes two fundamental factors. One is that to which I have referred, namely, representation by population. It is given priority but it is balanced to some degree by a consideration of region. It is recognized that in a country the size of Canada, made up of diverse communities and traditions, it is necessary there be adequate representation from all regions in the Parliament of Canada.
So we find that the membership of this House is based upon two factors, one population and the other region. It seems to me that the bill before us now is upsetting that balance. It threatens to give priority to region without adequate consideration to population. According to the British North America Act and according to the tradition

of this country, however, we have given priority to population change and population growth. It is for that reason the British North America Act contains a requirement that there will be redistribution following the census taken every ten years.
I can recognize the merits of the bill before us and appreciate the need for us to give proper consideration to some provinces and some regions of this country which, because of population decline, may be deprived of the representation to which they are entitled and which they need in order to voice adequately the aspirations of those areas. I certainly support that aspect of the bill. I suggest, however, it is incumbent upon this parliament to give adequate consideration and, indeed, priority to the population factor so that increased membership in this House of Commons is given to those areas where there has been such major population growth in the last ten years.
For example, we have, according to the membership of this House and the population of Canada, a situation by which the average population per riding is, I believe, in the neighbourhood of 83,000 people. Given the tolerance the legislation requires, by which an urban riding may be approximately 25 per cent above that, and a rural riding similarly below it, we should be having ridings which vary between a minimum of 60,000 and 100,000. We find, according to the 1971 census, there are 54 ridings in this country with a population of more than 100,000 people, 18 of which are in three metropolitan centres. Indeed, in the municipality to which I belong, the borough of Scarborough, there are two such ridings, one with a population of 193,156 and another, my own, with a population of 149,514.
On the other side, there are 43 constituencies each with a population of fewer than 60,000 people. Of these, eight have fewer than 50,000 people. Admittedly, some of these are required by certain constitutional requirements, but nevertheless there are others with fewer than 50,000 people in them. So we have a serious situation here which demands suitable correction as soon as possible to give adequate representation to these metropolitan areas where hundreds of thousands of people have congregated in the last decade. While wanting as far as possible to protect the interests and needs of those parts of Canada where population is declining, we must do justice to the areas where the majority of Canadians are living and working.
This is not a situation that is unique to Canada. We find that in the United States, where in the lower House membership to a large degree is based upon representation by population, similar changes are being made in the composition of the House of Representatives. According to population changes reported in the 1970 census, New York and Pennsylvania will lose two seats in the house, and Alabama, Iowa, North Dakota, Ohio, Tennessee, West Virginia and Wisconsin will lose one seat each. On the other hand, California will gain five seats, the state of Florida will gain three, and the states of Arizona, Texas and Colorado will each gain one.
We are therefore asking that more consideration be given to the large metropolitan areas of Canada where millions of people are now making their homes and contributing to the well-being of this country. We ask that
July 10, 1973

adequate representation be accorded these centres and that the membership of the House be adjusted accordingly. I hope this can be done in such a way that justice will be accorded to the massive population centres, and at the same time give just recognition to provinces and regions wherein the population rate has been declining but where there is also a need for adequate representation. Reference has been made to that need, certainly by the government House leader in his opening remarks in this debate. But I suggest that if we adopt the program that he outlined, we will not really come to grips with the situation. If we adopt uncritically the proposal in this bill, assuming that the next election is called some time before the end of 1974 it will be fought according to the old election map and the composition of the next parliament will be based on the population distribution of an out of date census. That means that if the parliament elected in 1974 were in office until 1978 or even 1979, we would come almost to the eve of the next census before there would be adequate reform in this area.
Therefore, I find quite inadequate the assurance of the government House leader in suggesting that he wants simply to stop the clock from ticking. It seems to me that he wants to turn back the clock and he wants the legislation to serve the Canada of yesterday rather than the Canadian people of today and tomorrow. I hope, therefore, that this bill, after passing second reading-as I think it is practical to assume it will-will be scrutinized carefully in committee. I hope we will then have the opportunity to introduce amendments that would give immediate recognition to the fair, just and necessary requirements of the major metropolitan centres of this country and, in particular, those provinces which according to the Electoral Boundaries Commission are due to receive increased representation.
I hope we can do that in such a way as not to deprive any province or region of that which it may need at this time in order to adequately represent in the House of Commons the needs and aspirations of its people and at the same time do justice to the people to whom I have referred.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to participate in the debate on Bill C-208, An Act to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act.
It was evident that the legislation suspending the operations of electoral boundaries commissions was absolutely necessary. Under that bill, the activities of those commissions are suspended until December 31, 1974.
Practically the only criterion selected by the commissions is population. They established a quota above or below in order that all ridings-rural or urban-have an equal number of voters regardless of the size of the riding.
On that basis, Quebec representation will decrease from 74 to 72 members in the House of Commons. This is unacceptable when we consider the principles and experiences which have been followed for more than 100 years for the establishment of electoral constituencies in Canada.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, that principle does not take into account the size of the riding when comparing the population of urban and rural constituencies.
On behalf of my constituents of Lotbiniere whom 1 am proud to represent in this House, I prepared and submitted myself a brief when the commission held a hearing in Trois-Rivieres. From the beginning-and I stated it clearly in my riding and in the House-I said that I would object strongly to the proposal of the commission which redistributes constituencies as it sees fit without taking basic factors into account.
I will try to deal briefly with some of those factors. First, the duty of a representative is in his riding. Mr. Speaker, the member of the electoral boundaries commission started with the principle that rural and urban constituencies have similar basic needs, which is false. They started from the principle that there is no real difference between a member for a rural riding and a member for an urban riding or a semi-rural, semi-urban riding, which is also false.
Mr. Speaker, when you select 83,000 voters, plus or minus 25 per cent, without taking account of the size of the constituency or its distance from the capital, you are infringing on the rights to fair representation of the people in that constituency.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is another fundamental principle which the members of the commission have not considered, namely the right of the people to obtain fair and effective service from their member of Parliament. And on this point I will say only this for now, that the standards for the role of the member of Parliament do not seem to have changed in over 100 years.
There was a time when sessions lasted for one, two or three months a year; the rest of the time the member of parliament spent in his constituency. That was tens of years ago. But today, in 1973, the member's time is divided between the work of the House, which has become increasingly burdensome, increasingly important, and the work in his own constituency, which must also not be neglected, for it is the basis of democracy, it is where the member of parliament draws his strength, gets his ideas, in short, it is what provides him with the whole meaning and value of his work.
Mr. Speaker, when any electoral boundaries commission sets constituency boundaries proportionately to the population, using demographic criteria and without considering the essential representational and organizational role which the member of parliament plays in his riding, then the boundaries which the commission in its ivory tower, may dream up, not only bear no relation to our daily lives, they also deprive the people of fair representation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, still in this connection, I wish to say that the services to the population entrusted to the member-I mean the secretaries, telephone lines, staff, equipment, etc.-should be allotted according to the size of the riding, its distance from the capital and specially its population.
Mr. Speaker, some considerations prompt me to oppose the work of the commission vigorously. In fact, on the

July 10, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
basis of the principles expressed a while ago, quite a distinction should be made between a rural and an urban riding, and a semi-urban riding, which distinction should be a factor of prime influence in redistribution.
Indeed, from a geographic point of view, the member does not have the same territory to cover, depending on the type of riding he represents. His work is very different, in terms of distances, if he represents an urban riding, Montreal, for instance, instead of a rural riding. As a result, equitable representation-and that is precisely what I will fight for most, for all the people, regardless of where they live in Canada-must not be based on the same national quota but on the geographic entity, cultural or other, of a riding.
Mr. Speaker, representing 83,000 people in an urban riding, and 83,000 people in a rural riding are two entirely different things. There is no need to dwell at great lengths on this subject. A study of the electoral map suggested by the commissioners will suffice to show the vast dimensions of rural ridings compared to those of the island of Montreal, for instance.
At this rate, if we continue to apply the same principle, in 20 years there will be more than twice the number of members for Montreal as for the rest of Quebec. The rural population already underrepresented, and this will only grow worse with the implementation of the false principle of the same quota indiscriminately across Canada.
I shall give an example which fits in well with the constituency I represent and those of Quebec as a whole. Let us first recall that the provincial quota proposed by the commission for Quebec is 83,719, which is completely ridiculous. It proves that the commissioners-and I shall say it plainly-have failed miserably to understand the member's role, the operation of the House of Commons or the basis of the distinction between constituencies, particularly between those of Quebec and those of the remaining parts of Canada. They have been, as we know it, dominating factors over the years.
Consequently, with this 83,719 quota, we find that Quebec has 26 constituencies which already exceed the quota in the new proposed redistribution. The commissioners propose a quota, a new electoral map and they already cheat on the quota in 26 constituencies. Out of these, seven extremely vast rural constituencies already top the proposed provincial quota. They are Temis-camingue, Roberval, Chicoutimi, Lapointe, Levis, Sherbrooke and Shefford. In this regard, Lotbinibre ranks 31st with 82,406 people.
What is most serious is that while wishing to set up a standard provincial quota, we already exceed it. In a territory of 50 by 60 miles in the Montreal metropolitan area, we have 2,782,738 people in 32 constituencies and a quota of 86,960. Note that out of 32 constituencies in this region 18 are already over the proposed quota before it is even adopted. Mr. Speaker, this shows that the passage of Bill C-208 would not represent a loss for us but rather a gain.
Now, if you consider, for comparison purposes, the region named in the table relating to Beauce and the Eastern Townships, that is to say ten constituencies, you will see that there are 815,891 people for ten ridings, and a

quota of 81,589. Therefore, you can see, Mr. Speaker, that the commissioners have not made any mental effort in establishing an equal quota, both for urban and rural constituencies.
Now, if you compare the size-which is extremely important from the view point of the member's work value-of this region to that of the preceding one, the region of Montreal, you may find right away that it is impossible for any hon. member to secure equitable representation for these people, on account of distances.
Mr. Speaker, these examples show that we must absolutely review the principle of equal quotas for rural and urban constituencies if we want fair representation in the House of Commons.
In order to comply with a pre-established quota, we must sometimes come to somewhat illogical divisions. And here are a few conclusions that we would have to come to if we relied on commissioners' genius, and we will find out that this does not make any sense. I will take as an example the constituency that I have the honour to represent, Lotbiniere.
If we followed the map pre-established by the commissioners, Lotbiniere would find itself divided into four regions with an entirely different mentality, in a kind of melting pot: Arthabaska and its region, Lotbiniere and its region, Nicolet and its region and finally, Megantic and its region. There, of course, the quota is exceeded. Conversely, Drummond would fall short. As the commissioners are mathematics experts, they decide to cut out Arthabaska which, however, is a natural entity. In order to comply with the quota, like in the urban constituencies of West-mount-because for them, there is no difference between an urban riding and a rural one-the commissioners remove Warwick, Saint-Albert and Daveluyville although those towns are quite close to Victoriaville. Thus, they break a cultural, economic, social and geographical entity in order to comply with a quota. The people of Warwick, Saint-Albert and Daveluyville live quite far from Drum-mondville compared to Victoriaville. Naturally, those people do business in Victoriaville. They very seldom have anything to do in Drummondville, except to visit friends or relatives.
Moreover, still in order to comply with this false principle of an equal quota for rural and urban ridings, two ridings are taken from Quebec, thus reducing its representation in Ottawa. The whole riding of Frontenac-in the neighbourhood of Lotbiniere-is being removed and half of it is incorporated in the new riding of Richmond and the other half, in Lotbiniere. It was already difficult to ensure a fair representation of those older ridings and now half of another is added to them. In the same manner 23 municipalities in the riding of Megantic are included in Lotbiniere.
The riding as proposed would cover an area of approximately 4900 square miles. For an area of roughly the same size, there are 32 ridings in Montreal and seven in Quebec City. Lotbiniere would also comprise over 57 municipalities.
In order to both guarantee a sound and equitable representation and ensure the preservation of a regional
July 10, 1973

identity-les Bois-Francs-I would on the other hand be pleased to have Plessisville included in this constituency, together with its sister towns; however, for the same reason, I humbly submit to the House that I am against this redistribution because it cuts off towns which have always had business relations with Victoriaville.
These are very local reasons; however, Mr. Speaker, if I am involved in politics, it is for the sake of Creditist principles. It is also because I could no longer agree with the concept of a member of parliament, as previously defined and as it appeared to apply in our constituencies at home: people, once elected, would disappear into thin air for the next four years, then show up again, come election time, to advise us that theirs was the best party and that we simply had to vote for them. Mr. Speaker, your people as well as ours are not dupe. In 1973, they want service from their member of parliament. They want a member who is able to meet them often, if necessary. They want a member who is available, they want to get in touch with him easily. That is why I work desperately to get the services that should be available to members of parliament in their respective ridings; that is why I object to this electoral map and, in particular, to the size of the ridings, the electoral quota, and the demographic and geographic factors that do not take into account cultural entities or the definition of the member's role.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to redistribute the seats in Quebec and in the rest of Canada to arrive at a given number of electoral districts, but when it is done overlooking the needs of the people, we rag them and, in this way, we merely help alienate them from parliament, from the member's role and from the member.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to say this, regarding, this legislation, with Bill C-208 which we will adopt and for which I will certainly vote, the commission's work will be suspended till December 31, 1974. I sincerely hope that by that time the members of all parties will have agreed to accept a new electoral map, if necessary, but only after having thought over the services made available to the members.
Mr. Speaker, suggesting a new electoral map without thinking over the services needed would be absolutely ridiculous, illogical and contradictory. For example, let us say that the ridings would change a little, and that new principles would tend to respect the standards I have enumerated.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Sainte-Croix-de-Lotbiniere, located 70 miles from Victoriaville, will still have difficulty contacting their representative. In addition those people pay taxes as do the people of Victoriaville. They need to meet with their member of parliament and I as a member, must meet with them in order to perform properly. But as long as this House act foolishly, as long as members of parliament are deprived of services in their ridings, briefly, as long as they are refused the necessary equipment to get closer to the people and the electoral map ignores them, the people will simply be divided and this once more will work towards keeping them apart from their representatives.
Mr. Speaker, I know that in the province of Quebec, the Lotbiniere riding has three provincial ridings. Each provincial member has two secretaries and one office in his
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension riding to serve part of the population. At the federal level Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but it seems to me that he has strayed considerably from the principle of the present bill. I must say that even when the hon. member was considering the electoral map in details, in as much as it affected his own electoral riding, he was then already out of order. The principle of the bill before us is very clear and I do not think that hon. members taking part in this debate should take advantage of the discussion on this bill to review the electoral map that has been submitted by various commissions.
The Standing Orders of this House and the legislation allow for debate to be held in due course on the electoral boundaries readjustment, but I think that hon. members are anticipating debate by using the bill under study to examine the electoral map in detail to the extent that it affects their own situation.
The hon. member is going even further beyond the framework of the debate when he invites this House to consider at the same times as this bill the services to be offered to members. It is clear to me that the hon. member is straying far from the principle of this bill, which is the only matter under study at the stage of the second reading.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree humbly and respectfully with your comments. However, I do not have to excuse myself for having considered the importance of the member's role while studying this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to continue my remarks but while I apologize to the Chair for departing from the Standing Orders, I wished to make those comments, though overtaxing your patience; but for me and many of my colleagues, this matter is extremely important.
I shall conclude by saying that a federal member represents three times more constituents than a provincial member and that he finds himself in an impossible position.
Those are the reasons why I am strongly opposed to the proposals of the Electoral Boundaries Commission and why I support this Bill C-208, hoping that from now on the commissioners wil draw their inspiration from more modern concepts that will be more realistic and that will meet the needs of the population, better than demographic criteria.
That is why, on behalf of my fellow citizens of Lotbiniere, Mr. Speaker, I wish to support this bill to suspend indefinitely the work of the commission and give the commissioners a well-deserved holiday as they made a big effort to draw an electoral map that will not hold water.

Mr. Speaker, I have read some of the speeches made in this debate and have listened to many others. Much has been said, but little of it has dealt with the problem before the House. Bill C-208 would halt redistribution as proposed by the legislation and refer the whole matter to a committee for further study. It certainly warrants further study, Mr. Speaker. Much argument has been made by members from some of
5464

July 10, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension the metropolitan areas that we must have "rep by pop". There is not a democracy, to my knowledge, functioning in a world that actually follows to the letter representation by population.
It is interesting to note that in his speech the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) referred at length to the American system and how they were having redistribution in the House of Representatives. Everybody in Canada knows that the powerful legislative body in American system is the Senate. He did not tell us how "rep by pop" really affected the American Senate. It does not affect it at all. The state of Alaska has two members, as has the state of New York; and there is a vast difference in their population. One wonders about the reason for this. The hon. member then referred to Great Britain and said that 200 years ago they came upon this problem and had to redistribute the seats in their country. He did not tell us what happened before 1832. They had representative government in Great Britain from 1264 to 1832. Not once in those 600 years did they have redistribution, so one can readily assume that in 1832 they needed redistribution.
Nobody in this House is opposed to the concept of redistribution. The question is, how often we should be subject to it and is it the proper time to proceed with it? That is the real question for the House. The hon. member for Scarborough East failed to deal with the problem as it affects Great Britain. He cited the arguments used in Great Britain which would substantiate his case, but he did not cite the whole case: they went from 1832 to 1918 with the only change being the one that was made in 1867. In the 1900s they had a redistribution committee and decided there should be redistribution not less than every three years and not more than every five years, but they found that was too difficult for the politicians and for the people to know their representative. Consequently it was amended to have redistribution not before ten years and not later than 15 years. They have gone the full limit of 15 years.
What has really taken place in that country? I think the significant thing is that even with that small, neat country in comparison to the vast region of Canada, they make special provisions for certain areas. The number of constituencies in Scotland and Wales must not be less than 71 and 35 respectively, and in Great Britain not substantially greater than 613. The book from which I quote, "Election in Britain", by R. L. Leonard, reads at the top of page 21:
This allocation gives more than their proportionate share of seats to Scotland and Wales, presumably as a sop to their national susceptibilities; conversely, Northern Ireland has less than its proportionate share, because its domestic affairs are dealt with by the Northern Ireland Parliament at Stormont.
Why do they give more than their proportion of representation to Scotland and Wales? Because they want Scotland and Wales to stay within that country; they want them to be governed by the parliament at Westminster.
Do we have a problem of national unity in this country? It has been mentioned from time to time in this House of Commons. A democracy must allow every region within the country an effective voice in parliament. A democracy must allow every segment within its society an effective voice in parliament. By segment I mean every industry whether it be agriculture, oil or any other. Every segment

of society must have an effective voice, or they will not be happy. Otherwise you merely breed discontent and alienation, and sometimes alienation precedes separation. What happened to Bangladesh? The people felt they did not have an effective voice in Pakistan and decided to separate from it. That is why in a democracy the people of various regions must be given an effective voice in parliament.
This country is composed of five main geographic regions. We must take care to allow each of those regions to have an effective voice. If any region feels that its voice is not effective, problems can arise-and there are problems in this country. That is why the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is meeting with the four western premiers. As Prime Minister of this country, he is aware of feelings of alienation in the west. There are some in this country who want to proceed with a redistribution bill that would further distort or destroy the partially effective voice that some regions now have. The number of seats in Newfoundland will be reduced from seven to six, and in Nova Scotia they are to be reduced to the bare minimum. Newfoundland is the newest part of Canada, having joined the country in 1949. Many people in Newfoundland still feel that was not a wise choice. If we continue to mute the effective voice which the province has had for the past 24 years, many in Newfoundland may experience growing feelings of alienation.
The same is true of the agricultural segment of our society. Some say that agriculture in this country is dying. Many in this House suggest that we should become a secondary manufacturing power. They think we may become an industrial nation second to none. There are some proponents of that philosophy in this country. They know that agriculture served this country in days gone by but think it will not hold an important place in Canada's future. I say to them, through you, Mr. Speaker, that agriculture will continue to play a prominent part in the livelihood of Canadians in the years ahead. Its part will be far more prominent than many in this House realize. The agricultural industry must maintain an effective voice in this House, otherwise it will feel alienated and will perhaps do something about that alienation. I do not think the agricultural regions should be depleted of members to represent them in this House.
The same holds true for other areas of endeavour in this country. Let us look at energy. There is an energy crisis in the world and the energy areas of Canada must be represented effectively in this House. Energy will be an increasingly important subject in the years ahead. One could list a whole host of such segments in our society. If we are to maintain our democracy as we now know it, we must make certain that those segments are given an effective voice in this House. Look back at what happened between 1911 and 1917 when western Canada was gypped, was beaten out of 22 seats: we were short of 22 seats for six years because of the influx of settlers from other parts of the country. Even if there is a redistribution of seats every ten years, the representation of certain areas will become distorted. The variations will be greater than 25 per cent; I do not deny that.

Consider Vancouver, for example. If it were not for the different products moving through that port, Vancouver would be much smaller than it now is. If it were not for the grains, oil, gas, coal, copper, iron ore, timber and other products moving from the interior of the country through that port, I suggest Vancouver would not be as big as it is today and not so many there would find employment. We talk about allocating representation. Let me say that Vancouver depends on the resource industries, although those industries do not make up that city. Certainly, some attention must be paid to those industries and to the other segments of our population which help to maintain our large metropolitan areas.
Under our constitution, the cities are the children of the provinces. Nevertheless, the resource industries are controlled and regulated by the Parliament of Canada. The wheat I sell and the price at which I sell it is controlled by this House. The amount of timber sold by this country is determined by this House, by this parliament. Incidentally, some have suggested that we should put an embargo on the sale of timber. Some suggest that we should have a two-price system for gas and oil. Those are decisions that are made in this House, not in any provincial house. Such decisions are the responsibility of this parliament and not the responsibility of any provincial, municipal or metropolitan government.
Consider, also, metropolitan Toronto. Members representing Toronto ridings complain that urban constituencies are growing too large. Let me say that Toronto is being maintained because of the purchasing power of certain areas outside Toronto. For instance, the farmers of western Canada buy much of their farm machinery in Toronto. They purchase over 50 per cent of their agricultural machinery there. Nearly all our conveyor belts come from the city of Toronto. As I say, many .of the large farm machines and many of the things farmers buy come from that city. Therefore, farmers help to maintain Toronto. At the same time, the way we sell our products and make our living is controlled by the policies of this government, not municipal or provincial governments. Therefore, I suggest that the agricultural industry and other segments of our society which make up this country should be given an effective voice in this House.
Look at the redistribution formula with respect to Alberta, as designed by the Electoral Boundaries Commission. No attention was paid to the 25 per cent formula. It is interesting to note that in a recent provincial redistribution, the commission involved gave Calgary and Edmonton about 37 per cent of the seats, although Calgary and Edmonton contain about 51 per cent of the population of Alberta. That commission paid a great deal of attention to the resource industries of the rural parts of the province.
In the matter we are now considering, Calgary and Edmonton were given over 57 per cent of the seats, and insufficient attention was paid to the rural areas of Alberta which greatly influence the prosperity of the province. Consider cattle. Whether cattle are to be sold and at what price they are to be sold are matters that are determined or influenced by this House. The same can be said of the sale of our coal, oil or gas. These sales are determined or influenced by members who sit in this House. I suggest that the Electoral Boundaries Commission has made an
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension error in Alberta. Of course, any action by this House in reviewing and examining effectively the concept behind the present legislation may be worth supporting. At the same time I ask, why should a rural riding have a population of approximately 96,000 while Calgary North has a population of 77,000? That just does not make sense.
A representative of the people in this House has two roles, two obligations to fulfil. He must act as ombudsman for his constituents and he must try to influence the action which the government will take so that it will be beneficial to his constituency and, hopefully, beneficial to the whole country. The member must become acquainted with his constituency. If he represents a large rural constituency which is sparsely populated, he will find it difficult to get around and meet all his constituents or even to make himself accessible to them. His task is far more difficult than that which faces members from a city riding whose population is contained within a certain number of blocks. To my mind there is no comparison between the difficulties which face them.
Regard should always be paid to the permitted variation of 25 per cent. I note that the hon. member for Scarborough East said he went along with this principle. He said some constituencies should contain a minimum population of perhaps 60,000 and the larger ones 100,000 or more. I go along with that. But the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Alberta in no way upheld that concept. There was only one constituency in which any variance was allowed, and that was Peace River where the commission allowed a variance of 12 per cent. From a cursory examination of other boundary commission reports across the country it appears a similar procedure was followed in other provinces. Indeed, the procedure is so similar one is bound to suspect that the whole system which was set up in 1964 has failed. At that time much thought was given in the debate here as to the way in which an independent body could be set up to decide these matters. One of the commission members was to be a judge, another was to be appointed by Your Honour. Another was to be the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly of the province in which the boundary commission was to be set up.
It should be borne in mind, too, that the Chief Electoral Officer of the day was to serve on each and every one of those commissions. Now, because of the similarity in the commission reports which becomes apparent upon studying them, one can only suspect that the main influence here was the former Chief Electoral Officer because in each province we find roughly the same type of approach to the 25 per cent variance principle. Hon. members who were here in 1964 will remember the lengthy discussion about whether there should be a 20 per cent variance or a 30 per cent variance. Parliament settled for a 25 per cent variance. The Electoral boundaries Commissions did not act in accordance with this intention, and we should therefore have no hesitation about setting aside the whole of these proposals and studying the matter again, in the hope of fashioning a system which will allow each area of Canada an effective voice in parliament and provide for a more satisfactory method of bringing about redistribution every ten years.

At the present time, members are faced with a good deal of uncertainty. They are not sure when the next election is likely to be because of the situation in which parliament finds itself, with a minority government. This surely warrants a ruling being made which would clear the air and avoid the possibility of members trying to represent, in effect, two constituencies; and this is what is likely to happen unless we clear the air for a certain period of time. For example, the judge appointed to the commission in the province of Alberta was a retired judge, 80 years old. I appeared before him and said I felt he had not done his duty; that he was, in effect, derelict in his duty because he had accepted a map drawn up in Ottawa. He never really denied that charge. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have grown accustomed to following the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) in debate, but never did I find myself so nervous, on the same side of the fence, as I am today. He might have. Mr. Speaker, when we deal with this subject as members of parliament we are dancing upon eggshells in terms of the fundamental principle of representation by population. The kind of argument advanced in support of this measure by the hon. member for Crowfoot would mean if followed to its logical conclusion, that six members of parliament would be sent to Ottawa by MacMillan Bloedel of the lumber industry and 17 MPs from Alberta would be sent by the Alberta oil companies. That is the kind of logic involved in the argument of the hon. member for Crowfoot. I wish to deal with the subject in a somewhat different vein.
The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse), in his argument, was very sanctimonious-maybe something he picked up in his previous profession-in insisting we must stick by the rule of representation by population to the bitter end. He ignored the fact that by the terms of the British North America Act and the manner in which redistribution is handled at the present time, we do not in fact stick by the principle of representation by population, inasmuch as the representation of certain provinces is not allowed to fall below a number prescribed according to the number of senators they have. That provision is put there to give some protection to the different regions of Canada.
My reasons for supporting this measure differ from those put forward by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the hon. member for Scarborough East. I feel time is necessary in which to consider the whole question of redistribution more broadly, including the total number of parliamentary seats which might have to be provided under redistribution, and the problem of provinces such as Saskatchewan which are faced with loss of representation. However, we ought not to allow members of parliament to become involved in any way with attempts to set aside decisions made by electoral commissions.
The over-all problem lies in the fact that the commissioners in the province of Saskatchewan, the province of Newfoundland and the province of Nova Scotia have been given the task of dividing constituencies on the basis of a reduced number, and every time they have to do this they must eliminate perhaps one constituency and extend the size of the others. So you have a situation in which a constituency such as mine before redistribution involved a land mass at least one-third or half the size of the country of Hungary, but following redistribution it will represent an area equal to the size of that country. That is the kind of situation that develops.
In three days travelling in my constituency from one community to another one can put 900 to 1,000 miles on his car. That is a tremendous amount of driving. There are tremendous problems of communication particularly as they relate to community of interest. To divide the area in this way we would have a new constituency of Moose Jaw-Assiniboia which would run from Davidson, Saskatchewan, down to the United States border. A constituency of that magnitude, represented by one member, is so large it would be impossible to give the service required of

the member. He must represent the views of the people in terms of those who live in the cities and those who live in the rural areas.
Most of us in Saskatchewan are adaptable and we are prepared to tackle this kind of problem, but if we continue along these lines the province of Saskatchewan could have its membership reduced to six. That is why there should be a review, rather than for the reasons advanced by the hon. member for Crowfoot, even though I am inclined to agree with some of them. We in Saskatchewan face the very definite possibility of having the number of representatives reduced to six.

This is a definite possibility, while at the same time the province of New Brunswick will be allowed to maintain its number of representatives at ten regardless of size of population. That is an extremely serious problem in terms of representation as enunciated by the British North America Act, and that is why I believe this review ought to take place. In addition, I believe the review ought to take place in a minority parliament rather than a parliament of majorities where one political party can hold the club in respect of the whole matter.
There have been arguments put forward by one of my colleagues from Saskatchewan. He said he was completely satisfied with the redistribution boundaries in the province of Saskatchewan. That is his right and prerogative. But during his argument he stated we were casting aside the work of the boundaries commissions across the country. To my mind that is an improper argument on this issue. We are not casting this work aside; we are suspending it for 18 months during which time we hope to reconcile our differences and develop a policy that is acceptable. Perhaps this will increase the number of members to something similar to the limitations in respect of the number of senators from each province. If we cannot answer these fundamental questions, then redistribution does in fact take place, regardless of what has been suggested by my colleague. He and I have had this debate in the corridor already, but I thought I should enunciate my feelings again.
I was amazed at the logic of some of the arguments of the hon. member for Peel South. He happens to be a Tory sitting close to me, but in terms of ideology he sits far away. After what I thought was an attack on the rural areas in relation to some mischievous plot that it taking place, pitting rural members against urban members, he went on to explain that Prince Edward Island should have six seats and that his urban area should have two representatives instead of one as at the present time. He then went on to say that with the recent growth rate, assuming this country would continue to grow at the same rate and that we would have the same number of constituencies, 264, based on the 1981 census Peel South would be entitled to four representatives.
The hon. member failed to point out that should the province of Prince Edward Island continue to lose population at the present rate-and I hope that does not happen-and fall below what is required for four constituencies, it would continue to have this number of members
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension regardless of population. He strenuously defended that position. Even if there was a loss in population, Prince Edward Island would be guaranteed that representation by the British North America Act. In this event, the people of Prince Edward Island would still have as much or greater representation than the increased representation the hon. member was suggesting for Peel South. The hon. member did not see in that situation a case for parliament reviewing the question of redistribution of representation by population, and for that reason I do not know why he opposes this measure.
Under this legislation we would in fact re-examine this very fundamental question in 18 months. We would not be re-examining the question of having independent boundaries commissions, which I think is a principle from which we should not wander. We would be re-examining the number of representatives in this House of Commons along with the ingredients that go into this whole matter of redistribution. We could examine the possibility of increasing the number of members in this House to avoid loss of representation in the provinces. We could go into many other matters at the same time. I think we should set ourselves that kind of job.
There is tremendous psychological reaction in many areas of this country which is difficult to explain to a member coming from a large urban area. There is psychological reaction in a rural area which has seen over the decades loss of population and loss of membership in this House of Commons. You can imagine the tremendous psychological effect of seeing 21 seats cut to 17, 17 to 13, 13 to 12 and then, as suggested to 11, 10, 9 or something of that order. I understand it would stop at ten in the province of Saskatchewan.
People would not react as strongly if they understood that even with the population growth there would be a limit on the increase in the number of members and they would stay at a certain level. But that does not take place under this legislation because we stay at a fixed number. If we stayed within the 25 per cent up or down adjustment rate, I think this would be a liberal approach to redistribution.
If we could redistribute in terms of considering the number of people it would be practical for an hon. member to properly represent, whether it be in an urban or a rural area, assuming that Canada's population continues growing, then consideration could be given not only to the rural members but to the urban members. If we keep the number of members at 264, assuming Canada's population continues to grow, then we must ask ourselves in respect of urban and rural centres how many people an hon. member should try to represent. I believe that a member, whether he lives in Peel South or Assiniboia, should not be asked to represent more than 30,000 or 35,000 voters. That would bring about an increase in the number of representatives.
What causes me concern is that after we drew up the British North America Act there were two systems of representation within parliament. One body was elected and the other was appointed. "The other," if I may remind members of the House, is the Senate. We do not hear very

But they tried at that time to bring in regional representation related to the United States system to which the hon. member for Crowfoot referred. They said there would be so many members from the prairie region, from the Maritimes, from Quebec, from Ontario, and so on. The other place has never lived up to the responsibility of giving regional representation, which supposedly was its task. It has been a most useless institution. It contains the greatest welfare cases we have ever had in this country from the time of drawing up the British North America Act.
I do not know exactly what the solution is to that problem. I suspect we could abolish the Senate and have more space for members of parliament. We could have representation by population so that there would be no need to do away with a constituency in Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan or Newfoundland. We would be able to increase the number of representatives those provinces have now, increase the number of members of parliament so they would be able to represent the people by election and not by appointment as a pay-off for duty well done to a government in Ottawa.
Therefore, I will support this bill on the basis of reviewing the general, over-all constitutional questions involved, but not in any way, shape or form in terms of any interference with the operation of the independent boundaries commissions which I believe are good and essential in principle.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my views on Bill C-208 to suspend the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. I support this legislation. I might add that I have represented the constituency of Marquette since 1968, which was the first election under the boundaries that exist for this riding. In the redistribution of 1966 the land area of Marquette almost doubled in size. On January 22, 1973, the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Manitoba announced its new proposals for Manitoba. Since that time I have received many letters from constituents in Marquette and other people in Manitoba expressing dissatisfaction with the proposals. I have also attended six meetings on redistribution in the riding since January 22.
Any Electoral Boundaries Commission dealing with redistribution has a very difficult task; it is impossible to please all areas of the country. However, I believe common sense has to be used. I have tried to obtain the reaction of the people of Marquette to the boundaries proposed and I say most emphatically that the present proposals are totally unacceptable to my constituents.
I feel it is most important that section 51 of the British North America Act be repealed and replaced by a new section in order to give recognition to area and regional representation of those provinces not protected by the senatorial floor to the extent that they should be. We believe it is most important that any committee set up to look into redistribution review this aspect completely. As an example, the province of Manitoba in 1941, with a population of just over 700,000, had 17 seats in the House of Commons. Under the proposals put forward this year by the Electoral Boundaries Commission, Manitoba which has a population of one million is to be reduced to 12 seats.
[Mr. Knight.)
In other words, in the last 30 years we have had an increase in population in Manitoba of well over a quarter of a million people, yet our representation in the House of Commons has been cut from 17 to 12 seats.
I want to list some of Manitoba's main concern regarding the present proposals. In the proposals, although the province loses one seat the commission has eliminated two rural ridings despite the fact that close to half our population still lives in rural Manitoba. I can see no reason for the rural areas losing two ridings. The redistribution act states that when you establish the population quota for a riding in a province you take the total population of the province and divide it by the designated number of seats in the province. In Manitoba's case, you divide 12 into the total population and the quota for a riding is approximately 82,000 people. The act states that because a metropolitan riding has a greater concentration of people it is allowed a tolerance of 25 per cent above this quota of 82,000. Because of the land area covered by most rural ridings they are allowed a tolerance of 25 per cent below the 82,000 quota.
The commission has completely disregarded the part of the act which provides that none of the rural ridings has to be above 65,000 population. The tolerance allowance was put into the act to protect the rural areas. The commission also seem to be assuming there will be the same depopulation of rural areas in the next ten years as there was in the last ten years. Most people feel there will be a levelling off and this trend will not continue to the same extent. In the proposals, only three ridings, Brandon-Souris, Churchill and Dauphin, do not touch greater Winnipeg. Of the other nine ridings, six are completely within the boundaries of greater Winnipeg and the remaining three border upon and enter the greater Winnipeg area. This means nine of our 12 ridings are connected to greater Winnipeg. This also means it is possible to have nine of the 12 members from Manitoba living in the greater Winnipeg area.
Another point I should like to make is that where possible we believe the commission should use natural barriers as boundaries. As an example, the northwest corner of the riding of Marquette has nothing in common with the riding of Dauphin. A large majority of the people in Marquette do not go to Dauphin once in ten years. In the case of Marquette, the majority of traffic moves in an east-west direction on the Trans-Canada Highway and No. 4 Highway. Between the cities of Brandon and Portage la Prairie there is very little traffic across the Assiniboine River. The proposals disregard completely natural travel patterns, trading areas and communities of interest.
We should also point out that Riding Mountain national park has over 1,200 square miles of wilderness. There is only one road across this park, No. 10 Highway, and it is controlled by the park authorities. There is presently talk that this highway may be turned into a scenic drive with a speed limit of 40 miles per hour, thereby eliminating all normal traffic.
In the proposed ridings of Dauphin and Portage, because of the way the population is evenly spread out it would be impossible for a member to give effective representation to these two new ridings because of them land area. Again, I mention the tolerance factor that is in the act to protect large rural ridings. At the time the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act was debated in the House of Commons,
July 10, 1973

it was clearly stated that full tolerance would be allowed to ensure that rural areas were fairly and properly represented. This is not the case under the present proposals. In the proposals for Manitoba the name of the federal constituency of Marquette disappears. Marquette has been the name of a Manitoba riding since confederation. In the early days Marquette was represented by Sir John A. Macdonald, our first Prime Minister. We feel that an historical name such as Marquette should be retained. This question should be taken into consideration whenever redistribution is discussed.
I want to make a very important point regarding the present commission. There are no representatives from the rural areas of Manitoba on the boundaries commission, and we feel strongly that all future commissions should include representatives from rural areas. Parliament, and the role of a member of parliament, have changed drastically in the last ten years. At one time the House of Commons was in session for only six months of the year and a member could spend six months in his riding communicating with and learning his constituents' problems. Today, the House is usually in session nine to ten months a year and being a federal member is definitely a full-time job. Citizens like to see their member of parliament and know the man who represents them. With the rural ridings being so large, this is impossible. As an example, in the 1971 summer recess I put 15,000 miles on my car in a two-month period touring the riding of Marquette, and even then I did not reach all parts of the riding. This is a ridiculous situation, yet under the proposals the rural ridings will increase again in size by half.
When the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson was prime minister he tried to bring Ottawa closer to the people. He made it possible for a member to take one air trip a week to his riding when the House was in session. Previously, only Ontario and Quebec members returned to their ridings regularly. One trip a week for all members meant that all areas of Canada were treated equally. However, for this system to work effectively rural ridings must follow natural travel patterns. In the new ridings of Dauphin and Portage, because of the area they cover and natural barriers it is virtually impossible to cover them effectively.
I should like to return to the reason the electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act provides that a rural riding can be 25 per cent below the normal quotient for a constituency in any given province, it is well known that a rural riding has many issues to contend with which come under federal jurisdiction and do not affect urban ridings to the same extent. I believe that the constituency of Marquette is a typical rural riding. Let us look at marquette and the areas of concern that face many rural ridings.
First, we have the Riding Mountain national park which creates many problems that face only rural areas. Second, in Marquette we have four Indian reservations. Admittedly, our native people face many problems in the cities, but there are no reservations in the urban areas. Third, in Marquette we have Camp Shilo. Usually, military training bases are located in rural areas because of the high cost of real estate and the large land area required. Fourth, transportation presents problems. In Marquette we have the Trans-Canada Highway and the Yellowhead route, two
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension transcontinental rail lines plus numerous branch lines which seriously affect the future movement of grain to world markets.
Fifth, although we border Lake Manitoba, commercial fishing does not affect Marquette as much as it does some rural ridings. However, in Marquette experiments have been conducted. Farmers' sloughs were stocked in the spring with fingerling trout and marketable fish were recovered from the sloughs in the fall. This has been called fish farming and we expect great development and advancement in this industry.
My last and main point concerns agriculture. Agriculture is still this nation's second largest industry. Because it is the nation's second largest industry and the fact that it takes huge areas of our country for this industry to function, it is imperative that farmers be given complete regional representation in Ottawa. As an example, urban areas are not concerned about the Canadian Wheat Board, PFRA, community pastures or the many other facets of agriculture. We must have representatives from the rural areas who understand these problems and can speak out for the farmer.
There are other points that I could make, but these are six reasons why the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act must protect the rural areas and give them fair representation in parliament. There is no reason under the act why any Manitoba rural riding must have a population of over 65,000. When the new proposals were announced for the province of Manitoba last January, because of the concern expressed by many people we felt that in order to keep the briefs non-political they should be presented to the hearings of the Manitoba Electoral Boundaries Commission by an elected representative at the municipal level of government. All mayors and reeves were contacted and meetings were held. This involved 41 councils which represented all the towns and rural municipalities in the constituency of Marquette.
It is a clear fact that by resolution or by presenting a brief at the commission hearings in either Portage la Prairie or Brandon, all 41 councils opposed the proposed boundary changes. It must be a unique situation in Canada when all municipal councils in one constituency oppose boundary changes. At the time of the Manitoba commission hearings in Brandon I asked that the present proposals be scrapped and protection be given to the rural areas of the province. It is only fair that we protect the rural way of life, a way of life that is cherished by many. As pointed out by many other speakers, most countries give recognition to area and regional representation. I feel that Canada must do this, and I support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, my participation in this debate marks the fourth or fifth time that I have taken part in debates in the House of Commons since the House began its sittings in January. Other members have spoken much more than me. I have deliberately remained in my seat during several of the debates because I believe that, as a new member, one of the most important things I can do here in Ottawa is to learn more about the issues which affect our country so that any contribution I make to our deliberations can be reasoned and coherent. However, from time to time issues arise that require a member of

July 10, 1973

This bill to postpone the proposed new redistribution is one of those issues. Over the past few days we have heard several speakers from all parties putting forward major arguments both for and against postponing redistribution and I have followed the debate with interest. I would like to add my voice to those members who have spoken against immediate redistribution of electoral boundaries.
As a rural member of parliament, the validity of the case against redistribution is apparent to me. Many of the arguments used in defence of our position are well known. I used them myself in my presentation to the federal Electoral Boundaries Commission earlier this year. The demands upon rural and urban members are different, and communications within an urban riding are often much easier than within a rural constituency stretching over several hundred square miles. It takes time for a rural member to win the recognition and trust of his constituents on a person to person basis, which is important if he is to serve them properly. The minorities-the young, the old, the poor, and the ethnic groups-can all be brought into full participation in our democracy, but it takes time and stability for this to be done.
Regular redistribution merely serves to destroy much of the work that a conscientious member of parliament does between elections. Areas without any community of interest are regularly placed together in a new constituency, and by the time they begin to work together as a unit they are again torn apart. Redistribution often means that a rural area which was once represented by a rural member of parliament finds itself submerged by the much greater numbers in an urban area to which it is joined in redistribution. This particular phenomenon will take place in my home town if redistribution goes through as planned.
All these arguments are valid and in themselves afford ample justification for the postponement of redistribution. But today I would like to address my remarks to the contention of some urban members that those of us who oppose redistribution are somehow undemocratic. In any debate of this kind we hear the proponents of redistribution say that rural areas are already vastly over-represented, that on the basis of representation by population it is apparent that rural constituencies have been getting more than their share of power in government. It is this claim that we have been getting too much representation that I would like to discuss.
I do not think anyone here today would try to deny the fact that the number of voters in a rural constituency in this country is often much smaller than in urban constituencies. Certainly, I would not. It would appear from a superficial analysis of representation in Canada that rural Canadians like myself have a great deal more say than our numbers entitle us to have. But the people who are satisfied with these assertions refuse to look beyond the most superficial level. If we want to see which group really dominates government in Canada, we should not be looking at those of us who sit in the back benches but, rather, at those who sit in the front rows: members of the cabinet, the shadow cabinet, and the leaders of our national parties. The vast preponderance of this group is urban. They represent urban constituencies. They had urban jobs
[Mr. Beatty (Wellington-Grt?y-Dufferin-Waterloo).j
before they were elected, and they were given an urban education. Their way of viewing the problems of Canada is urban, and their priorities are urban priorities.
About all that rural Canadians can be assured of being able to claim on the front benches is the Department of Agriculture and the chairmanship of the various agricultural committees of party caucuses. And it was not very long ago that even the Minister of Agriculture represented an urban seat. The power within the House of Commons is already in the hands of urban members. But what about the other aspects of government, the political parties and the civil service? The answer to that question is just as simple. Our political parties are run from the cities by people who live in the cities, who take advice from urban advisers, who received urban educations, who collect money from urban businesses and urban unions and who contract for work to be done by urban suppliers. They often wear blinders in respect of the needs of rural party members.
Our bureaucracy in Canada is centred in Ottawa and in the other large cities. The people who dominate the Treasury Board, who design our economic strategy and who run the various departments and agencies of government are not rural Canadians. They come from the cities. They often have an urban contempt for rural people and their problems. Yet we hear that rural Canadians dominate our governments and they must be further stripped of whatever influence remains to them in government.
Unquestionably, some of the members of this House are dubious about the ill effects that can be caused for rural Canadians by having decisions made in the cities. Anyone who doubts the implications of urban control of government need only look at programs such as Opportunities for Youth, LIP and those under the Canada Council to discover that the lives of rural Canadians are being shaped, not by their local councils which are responsive to their needs and their desires, not by their members of the federal or provincial parliaments but by bureaucrats in Ottawa or in the other cities who systematically bypass local governments and determine for themselves what is in the best interests of rural Canadians. And as the cost of the government and the scope of its activities grow, the power of rural Canadians to live their own lives in freedom and to develop in their own way grows less and less.
Perhaps the creeping impotence of that part of Canada beyond the borders of our great cities is best symbolized by the federal task force on agriculture that was composed, not of farmers-because farmers would not be capable of planning for the future of agriculture-but by four academics and one chartered accountant. In their recommendations they constructed a 1990s model of agriculture that would drive even more family farmers from business and encourage even further rural depopulation. That report, commissioned by the federal government, would be the death sentence of rural Canada if it were implemented.
The argument that rural Canadians are being undemocratic in opposing an even greater shift of political power to the cities might make more sense if all that we had to consider was the structure of government. But if we are
July 10, 1973

serious about examining the structure of power in Canada we have to look beyond government to the other institutions that condition and shape our lives. Industry and commerce are centred in the cities. With them remain the wealth and opportunities to be found within business. Our great labour unions are urban institutions. Education, in the form of post-secondary schooling and in the regulation of our schooling systems, is centred in the cities.
The media and communications are located in the cities. Even what goes into our daily newspaper is reported by people from the cities on the basis of their urban news judgment. And because the major markets are in the cities, items of interest to rural Canadians are often ignored. Transportation facilities are located in the cities. In my area of Ontario we do not even have passenger train service.
Cultural facilities and artists are to be found in the cities. The recognition of the role which artists play in determining our national heritage is based upon urban criteria. How many Canada Council grants have gone to rural organizations? When was the last time that a country music singer was asked to dine at 24 Sussex Drive? They are excluded because of a sense of cultural elitism on the part of the people who decide what constitutes culture, despite the fact that for millions of Canadians country music is part of their lifestyle. As our society has become centralized and bureaucratized, rural Canadians have become forgotten Canadians. Many of my friends in politics are from the cities, and they tell me that they want to participate in the cities because the great problems of the next few decades will be urban problems which will require urban solutions. How myopic can they be?
We have set in motion a chain of events which will serve to destroy rural Canada and which can only worsen the problems of the cities unless it is stopped. Almost every three hours another rural Ontarian leaves the farm because the economic cards are so badly stacked against the family farmer. And as the rural townships depopulate, the community school and church are closed and the general store is forced to close its door. Because the rich people from the cities, who buy up the farms for use as weekend retreats, do their shopping in the city and refuse to make improvements on their land or to township roads, the small stores in the rural communities are closed and township councils are unable to provide the level of services that are necessary to keep their areas viable.
As the rural people leave the farms in search of new opportunities, they migrate to the cities where they only add to the problems of unemployment, of welfare, of housing, of transportation, of pollution and of policing. How much cheaper would it have been for our society to keep the rural areas vital and healthy than to have to deal with the results of their neglect when they are felt in the cities? And what are the social costs of uprooting rural Canadians from their lifestyle of decades and forcing them to adapt to the way of life in the collection of expressways and neuroses that we call cities? Joni Mitchell, the Canadian folksinger, described the situation well when she said:
And on and on we seem to go
That you don't know what you've got till it's gone

And put up a parking lot.
The time has come in Canada to start to decentralize power in Canada, to return it to the small communities and to the people of this country. The time has come for a rebirth of democracy in this country.
True democracy does not lend itself to neat formulas based upon the domination by a large and powerful group over a smaller and powerless one. It means the right and ability of all people, regardless of wealth, family background or geography, to freedom and dignity, the right to live their own lives in peace. I turned my back on a career in the city that might have been easier and more prosperous and returned home to run for political office because I believe it is about time somebody started to speak out for small towns and rural Canada. I think it is about time that rural Canadians were again given a chance for a decent life. It is about time a major political party in this country repudiated the policies of successive administrations that have centralized power in our society and disenfranchised the average Canadian, whether he lives in the cities or in the country.
The issue is not one of an antiquated way of life passing into history. It is one part of the struggle to maintain and restore those elements of humanity that still remain in a technological culture that is so often coldly brutal and inhumane. It is the struggle for the right to be ourselves. Rural Canadians love this country and we believe in its future. We want our children to have a part in Canada's future. That is what this whole debate is really about.

Redistribution in a country such as Canada is not going to be easy. The demographic trends make it extremely difficult. Regional disparities in our country make it extremely difficult. No one is going to suggest that whatever formula we come up with will meet 100 per cent approval.
I think that in my province of British Columbia, within the parameters of the act under which it must function, the redistribution committee did a pretty good job. Certainly the members of the commission did not please everyone, but any representations that were made to them, at least when it was present, including ones I made myself, were listened to thoughtfully and I think resulted in changes along the lines of the suggestions made.
